newsitem.title: USA: Risky U.S. mission left plutonium in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Risky U.S. mission left plutonium in Vietnam.

text.p: Americans on a risky rescue mission left a canister of plutonium, a key ingredient of nuclear bombs, in Vietnam as the communists marched to victory in 1975, the Energy Department disclosed on Wednesday.

Releasing once-secret documents on the 80 grams (about three ounces) of missing plutonium, the department said U.S. officials were working with the International Atomic Energy Agency to verify its status "and take any necessary action."

"The volume of plutonium and circumstances involved do not give rise to special proliferation concerns," it said in a statement at a news conference marking the declassification of more than 6,500 films chronicling the atomic age.

The statement said Vietnam, a signatory to the treaty aimed at curbing the spread of nuclear weapons and a member of the Vienna-based IAEA, had been "responsive" to U.S. State Department inquiries about the plutonium, said by experts to be too small an amount to build a bomb.

The United States sent the plutonium to the South Vietnamese government in 1962 for use in a research reactor in the central highlands resort city of Dalat under the "Atoms for Peace" programme, an Energy Department fact sheet said.
It said the material apparently was still at Dalat, where Vietnam reactivated the U.S.-supplied reactor with help from the former Soviet Union, which provided enriched uranium fuel.

The IAEA plans to inspect the Dalat facility next month to check whether a Vietnamese plutonium source on its records matches the one left behind by the United States at war's end, the fact sheet said.

The newly declassified documents showed that two U.S. volunteers on a James Bond-style cloak-and-dagger mission had reached Dalat in late March 1975 to recover highly enriched uranium fuel and the plutonium. At that time Dalat was encircled on three sides by Viet Cong guerrillas and North Vietnamese regular forces.

Toiling as sniper fire ricocheted through the reactor area, the pair mistakenly retrieved a similarly sealed radioactive alloy, leaving the stainless steel-clad container with the plutonium behind, the account said.

A declassified memorandum identified the pair, who received commendations for wartime valour, as Wally Hendrickson and John Horan, both from the Idaho operations office of the Atomic Energy Commission, forerunner of the Energy Department.
While in Dalat on their mission, "nearby combat was occurring and sniper bullets were hitting the reactor area," the fact sheet said.

By the evening of April 1, Hendrickson, of Coeur d'Alene, Idaho, and Horan, of Idaho Falls, Idaho, were being flown back to Saigon, thinking they had accomplished their mission and retrieved the plutonium. In fact, Hendrickson said in an interview on Wednesday, he had mistakenly grabbed not the plutonium but a relatively harmless alloy of polonium and beryllium. Dalat fell to the Viet Cong that night.
Asked how he and Horan had been chosen for the mission, Hendrickson, now 62 and working on nuclear cleanup issues, said they were apparently alone among their thousands of co-workers to volunteer.

"We were willing -- that was the major criteria," he said from his office in Richland, Washington. He added that he and Horan, who also still works for the Energy Department, had no background in spycraft or covert operations.
Hendrickson said he and Horan had been warned by U.S. embassy officials in Saigon at the time that they would be on their own if Dalat was overrun while they were there.

O'Leary said the episode, including updating the official U.S. inventory of plutonium and records on file with the IAEA, came to light during routine declassification review of old documents under rules established by President Bill Clinton.
